text.p: Drinks group Guinness Plc posted an 11 percent rise in 1996 pretax profits to 975 million pounds ($1.56 billion) on Thursday, and chairman Tony Greener made positive remarks about the trading climate for its spirits brands.
"We have seen in developed markets, and particularly in the United States, the start of a turnaround, for the first time since the early 1980's," he told Reuters in an interview.

Sales volumes at United Distillers (UD), the company's spirits arm, rose one percent in 1996 to 45.7 million cases, an increase of 0.6 million on 1995. UD achieved an overall average price increase in the year of around 1.5 percent and Greener made positive remarks about the climate for pricing in the coming year.
"Going forward our feeling is the climate for pricing is improving and in terms of Scotch (whisky) volume we would expect to see the underlying rate of growth on Scotch sales improving again."
Greener said the company had already announced a number of price increases for the coming year, "Our sense is the overall climate for price increases will be somewhat more favourable this year."
Scotch whisky sales at 25.7 million cases were one percent below the comparable 1995 level due to deliberately reduced shipments designed to reduce trade stock levels.
"Sales of Johnnie Walker Black Label were up by six percent. So we are really seeing a good strong performance at consumer level in the States which I really think is encouraging," he said.
The company has announced a two percent price rise in the United States, due to come into effect on July 1, for chain stores and February 1 for controlled states.
In Thailand a 1.2 percent rise has been announced and in Japan a two percent increase due on April 1, although prices in Japan were adjusted down by four percent last year.
Asia Pacific profits rose 15 percent to 184 million pounds in 1996, making it the UD's largest profit region.

However, conditions in mainland Europe, especially Germany and France, remain tight, Greener said. In Spain and Portugal the company aims to get price rises of between three and four percent through on its spirits brands with effect from June 1. In Germany, a three percent rise on Johnnie Walker is planned for the second half of the year.
"The U.S economy, being strong, is very helpful although in Europe, progress remains slow and we do not expect a big consumer bounceback in Germany and France," Greener said.
"In the UK the strategy is to build the equity of our brands and lead the industry on a stronger pricing environment and we have had some good success in both of those areas last year," he said.
Prices on UD's spirits brands in Britain were increased seven percent last year. The company also held prices ahead of Christmas when the temptation is strongest to offer discounts, Greener said.
Profits from Britain fell nine percent to 49 million pounds in 1996 after a big increase in marketing and the company's decision to scrap promotional offers.
Guinness spent 330 million pounds on marketing at UD last year and 205 million on Guinness brewing and this double digit year-on-year increase will continue.
"I have called it a landmark year because its a year in which a lot of the action and investment we have been taking over the last few years has started to come through," Greener said.
United Distillers turned in a fairly flat performance with trading profits of 678 million pounds in 1996, while brewing recorded a six percent rise to 283 million.

Brokers had predicted profits would fall into a range of 960 to 965 million pounds and the dividend of 16.1 pence per share was narrowly firmer than the average analyst prediction of 16.0. The company's shares rose eight pence to 494 in morning trade. ($1=.6271 Pound)
